title: The Holy Innocents (28 December)
hook: the children killed by Herod; a day for all suffering children

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Stephen, chosen to feed the widows, and a king carrying food through the snow. Your line was the feast of stephen. Did your food reach someone's door? Day one thousand thirteen.

Not every Christmas carol is cheerful. There's an old English one, a lullaby, sung in the voice of the mothers of Bethlehem, rocking their babies and knowing what's coming. It's gentle and it's terrible at the same time. A few days after Christmas, the church calendar stops the celebration and remembers something nobody would put on a greeting card: the children of Bethlehem killed on the orders of a frightened king. The day is quiet. In some churches the vestments turn red, the color worn for martyrs, and in some it has become a day to pray for every child who suffers. Today, the Holy Innocents.

Matthew's Gospel tells it. Wise men from the east come to King Herod asking where the newborn king of the Jews is. Herod is alarmed. He sends them on to Bethlehem and asks them to report back. They find the child, and then, warned in a dream, go home another way. In the King James Bible, Herod "saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth." He sends out orders to kill the children of Bethlehem. Joseph, warned in a dream too, has already fled with Mary and the child into Egypt. The child escapes. The others don't. Then Matthew reaches back to the prophet Jeremiah: "In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Rachel is one of the mothers of Israel, Jacob's beloved wife, and Genesis says she was buried near this very town: "And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem." So Matthew pictures the old mother crying from her grave over the children of her own town. And look at the words: would not be comforted. The text doesn't hurry her. It doesn't explain the deaths or tidy them up. It lets her grief stand. Perhaps that's why the church keeps the day the way it does. Tradition calls the Holy Innocents holy not because of anything they did, but because they died, children, in the shadow of the story of Jesus. And so the day reaches out to every child caught in someone else's fear and violence, in war, in hunger, in harm at home. In the text, Rachel is still weeping. The day asks the church to weep with her.

Here's the practice: let one suffering child have your attention. Settle, and breathe. Maybe a face from the news. Maybe a child you know who's having a hard time. Maybe just the children of one place you've heard about this week. Don't rush to fix the feeling. Let it be heavy for a moment, the way Rachel's grief is allowed to be. Then choose one children's charity you could give to, even a little, today. If you pray, you can hold those children before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and stay with them. The bell holds the time.
Herod. The frightened king whose orders killed the children of Bethlehem, remembered on this quiet day just after Christmas.
Your line: rachel weeping. Today, give what you can to the children's charity you chose, and don't hurry past the grief it answers. Day one thousand thirteen.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches keep the Holy Innocents a few days after Christmas, and the Orthodox remember them on their own calendar; some churches use the day to pray for children who suffer, and some bless children at the service.

original.note: Hebrew: Rachel — one of the mothers of Israel in Genesis, weeping for her children in Jeremiah 31:15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad side story in the Christmas pageant.
what it means: the children of Bethlehem killed by Herod, remembered for every child who suffers.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 2:18 quoting Jeremiah 31:15 — and Genesis 35:19 burying Rachel on the way to Bethlehem.

notes: Claims rule: no number of children, no age range (Matthew 2:16 gives one; left out), and no historical claim about other sources for the event.
The 'old English lullaby' is the Coventry Carol; not named or quoted, and no date given. Confirm the description.
Vestment color 'turns to the color of grief' is kept vague (some churches use violet or red); confirm.
Care with history: Herod is the actor; no group blame. Confirm.
Orthodox commemoration date (29 December on their calendar) described only as 'on their own calendar'.

Editor: Matthew 2:16 names no soldiers and says 'children', so 'soldiers' and 'little boys' were changed; why they are called holy is now attributed to tradition; 'Rachel is still weeping' tied to the text.
Editor 2: Rachel is now 'one of the mothers of Israel' (Genesis also gives Leah, Bilhah and Zilpah as mothers of Jacob's sons); 'that's why the church keeps the day' softened with 'perhaps'.

Audit: hook comma splice ('The day is quiet, sometimes the vestments...') rewritten; 'the color of grief' was inaccurate for the current Roman rite (red, for martyrs; violet in older use), now 'red, the color worn for martyrs' in some churches. Practice dropped the doubled 'until the bell. The bell holds the time.'
